HyCo: Hybrid Drafting for Cost-Efficient
Mobile–Cloud Speculative Decoding

Hanbin Bae    Heejin Choi    Joohyung Lee Affiliation: Byoung Jin Choi   Sangjun Park   Hoon-Young Cho Affiliation: AI Solution Team, Samsung Research, Seoul, Republic of Korea Email: {bhb0722.bae,hee_jin.choi,jooooh.lee,bj87.choi,sj0.park,h.y.cho}@samsung.com
Abstract

Device–cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which assigns depth to the server model’s native multi-token prediction (MTP) head, executed on the device, and alternative branches to one SLM pass. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key–value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An ϵ\epsilon-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier’s sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three Spec-Bench runs per system show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9×1.9\times delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2+0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: −0.9-0.9 to +1.3+1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.

1 Introduction

Speculative decoding accelerates large language models (LLMs) by verifying several draft tokens in one forward pass, with exact verification preserving the LLM’s sampling distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). Serving engines support it (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024), and recent LLMs include a native multi-token prediction (MTP) head (DeepSeek-AI, 2024; Gemma Team, 2026), one of several approaches to drafting from the LLM’s hidden states (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b). Device–cloud speculative decoding instead places a small language model (SLM) on the user’s device and leaves verification to the server (Park et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a). Communication can make an individual request slower than server-only speculation (Lyu et al., 2026); the opportunity is therefore to reduce server computation without making the mobile experience impractically slow.

We target two goals. The server should spend less GPU time per output token than Cloud+MTP, which already runs the LLM’s own MTP self-speculation. The user should receive tokens at least as fast as the SLM alone generates them on the device. These are distinct reference points: Cloud+MTP measures the server-side opportunity, whereas the SLM alone represents a local alternative for the user.

Meeting both goals is difficult on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). The drafters must fit integer execution graphs, limited shared memory, and compiled context lengths. Acceptance varies across tasks (Liu et al., 2024a; Xia et al., 2024) and determines how effectively each round amortizes server work and communication. A tree offers alternative tokens at each position and is verified in one pass (Miao et al., 2024), but growing it with an autoregressive SLM requires a sequential pass per level. The four-level SpecEdge-style tree studied here raises the mean number of tokens accepted per round (MAT), yet its four mobile SLM passes leave the user slower than the SLM alone. The challenge is to obtain useful depth and alternatives without repeatedly running the SLM.

We present HyCo, based on a division of drafting work. The LLM’s native MTP head reads only a small slice of the LLM’s state, so it can execute on the mobile device. This MTP Drafter supplies a chain that gives the tree its depth. The server’s LLM, the verifier , returns the head’s inputs with each verification rather than executing the head’s sequential steps itself. One pass of the device’s SLM Drafter adds alternatives under the root and every planted node, allowing the tree to continue where the chain breaks. Together, the two form the Hybrid Drafter , whose output is the hybrid draft tree. The MTP head still runs sequentially, but depth no longer requires extra SLM passes.

Integer quantization, a restricted output vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU, at some cost in acceptance. On the server, ϵ\epsilon-threshold acceptance additionally accepts drafted tokens whose probability under the verifier’s sampling distribution reaches ϵ\epsilon (Hewitt et al., 2022). This raises acceptance but changes the output distribution. We therefore evaluate quality alongside server GPU time, mobile draft time, and user delivery speed, and compare both an exact-verification ablation and an SLM-only tree under the same threshold.

We evaluate Gemma 4 26B-A4B on an RTX PRO 6000 cloud GPU, with its MTP head and Gemma 4 E2B on a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G. In single-client measurements, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token against Cloud+MTP by 38.6% on Spec-Bench (Xia et al., 2024, SB;) and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization from ∞\inftyBench Sum (Zhang et al., 2024). On SB, three runs of both HyCo and the SLM-only baseline under the same ϵ\epsilon rule give reductions of 38.6±0.238.6\pm 0.2% and 29.6±0.229.6\pm 0.2%, respectively. HyCo delivers 35.0 tokens/s, 1.9×1.9\times the baseline’s rate and faster than the SLM alone. With exact verification, HyCo still saves 27.7% and 11.9%, respectively. Repeated generation and long-summary assessment characterize the quality trade-offs. Our contribution is the native-head/SLM division of drafting work and an implementation demonstrating its usefulness under mobile NPU constraints.

2 Related Work

Work on device–cloud speculative decoding either strengthens the draft or skips verification where the device is confident. The draft is strengthened in three ways: drafting a tree instead of a sequence (Miao et al., 2024; Park et al., 2025), training the draft model toward the target (Zhou et al., 2024), or drafting several tokens in parallel (An et al., 2026). The latter two retrain the draft model and are orthogonal to our approach: HyCo keeps its drafters as released, apart from quantization and a restricted output vocabulary, and strengthens the draft through its tree.

In SLM-based device–cloud systems, the device’s draft model drafts every proposed token (Park et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026c), one sequential pass per tree level, and SpecEdge overlaps these passes with the round trip by proactive drafting (PD), preparing the next round’s tree while the reply is in flight.

Among the device–cloud systems in Table 1, none drafts with the LLM’s native draft head: HAT (Xie et al., 2026) runs the LLM’s first layers on the device, whereas Li et al. (2026a) draft from hidden states returned by the server . Cloud+MTP drafts with that head, but on the server. HyCo instead runs that head on the mobile device, beside one SLM pass.

Skipping verification by confidence saves rounds but is lossy. Synera keeps on the device the tokens whose confidence clears a threshold and offloads only the rest for the cloud to verify (Wang et al., 2025) . The cloud’s LLM does not check the locally retained tokens. HyCo instead checks every round with the verifier and raises acceptance within that check through ϵ\epsilon-threshold acceptance; its relaxed rule is also lossy.

Raising acceptance within verification is the aim of lossy acceptance rules, which accept drafted tokens that the target would not necessarily sample, and they differ in what they test. BiLD keeps a small model’s tokens unless its distribution diverges from the large model’s beyond a threshold (Kim et al., 2023), and fuzzy speculative decoding and the edge–cloud E2-SCI accept within divergence thresholds of their own (Holsman et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b). Judge decoding lets a learned judge keep tokens that exact verification rejects (Bachmann et al., 2025), and Medusa’s typical acceptance tests the target’s raw softmax against an entropy-adaptive threshold taken from η\eta-sampling (Cai et al., 2024; Hewitt et al., 2022).

HyCo’s ϵ\epsilon-threshold acceptance instead thresholds the verifier’s own sampling distribution p~\tilde{p} (§3.5) .

3 Method

In HyCo, the mobile device constructs a hybrid draft tree and the server’s verifier checks it (Algorithm 1). We measure and compare settings on UC-val, 60 prompts from the test split of UltraChat 200k (Ding et al., 2023; Tunstall et al., 2024, UC;), and fix the chosen configuration for the reported SB and ∞\inftyBench Sum runs (Appendix D) . Server cost gg is the total GPU time including prefill divided by output tokens. For decoding, this is server time per round divided by MAT.

The default selection criterion minimizes gg among settings whose LLM-judge score (§4.3) falls within the observed lossless-run range, 58.7–63.0. This is a screening heuristic, not a quality-equivalence test: two runs of the same setting scored 57.1 and 61.5 . When gg differs by less than the approximately 2% variation observed in validation, we use the stated device-cost or comparison rationale .

3.1 Hybrid draft tree

Figure 2 depicts one round, from the verifier’s hand-off to its check of the trimmed tree. The MTP Drafter is the verifier’s own MTP head, quantized by our quantization-aware training (QAT), and drafts each round’s chain of KK top-1 tokens, which gives the hybrid draft tree its depth. It reads the input embedding e⁡(xt+1)e(x_{t+1}) of the tree’s root xt+1x_{t+1}, the last hidden state hth_{t} from which the verifier sampled xt+1x_{t+1}, and the keys and values (KV) of two verifier layers . The server returns these inputs with each verification, 5.6 KB per round plus 6.1 KB per output token at 8 bits, and skips the KK sequential steps that its MTP head runs after every verification pass in Cloud+MTP . Running the MTP head on the mobile device instead of the server shortens the server’s median round from 26.8 to 21.7 ms and lowers gg by 15.2%, at about 20 ms more per round on the mobile device .

At its first two steps, the MTP Drafter also plants its second-ranked token beside the chain token as a runner-up sibling, in case the top-1 misses the verifier’s choice . The SLM Drafter, Gemma 4 E2B from Google’s QAT checkpoint (Google DeepMind, 2026), then proposes in one pass children under the root and every planted node, giving the tree its width. Trimming the tree to its node budget needs scores that weigh the chain’s nodes, which carry no probability, against the SLM’s candidates.

Each depth along a node’s path costs ln⁡0.66≈−0.42\ln 0.66\approx-0.42, as the chain’s acceptance rate per depth, the share of rounds whose first kk chain tokens are all accepted among those whose first k−1k{-}1 are, is 0.65–0.68 at every depth, with a geometric mean of 0.66 . A depth-dd chain node thus scores d​ln⁡0.66d\ln 0.66, about the logarithm of its chance of being accepted. A runner-up sibling pays this cost twice on its own edge, which ranks it just below the chain token it doubles, and an SLM candidate adds its token’s log-probability to the cost . The tree is then trimmed by score, closed under ancestors, and sent as token IDs and parent indices, 2.2 KB per round . The verifier checks it in one forward pass with a tree attention mask (Miao et al., 2024). Under exact verification, it samples at each node vv from its sampling distribution p~(⋅∣v)\tilde{p}(\cdot\mid v) and descends to the matching child, so the committed text follows p~\tilde{p} and verification is lossless. The first sample that matches no child ends the round as its bonus token, which MAT counts and which becomes the root of the next tree.

The chain supplies most accepted tokens, and the siblings and the SLM’s alternatives take over where it breaks. An SLM leaf extends a fully accepted chain to a fifth token in 17% of rounds under exact verification .

We choose K=4K{=}4 and runner-up siblings at depths 1–2 on UC-val. The cumulative chain acceptance reaches 18.9% at depth 4; later siblings bring little additional server saving. The 32-node budget matches SpecEdge-style, and the verifier uses the same 33-row CUDA graphs, including the root. A second SLM pass is retained as the HyCo-2P operating option rather than the default (Appendix D).

3.2 Quantization

Integer graphs let both drafters exploit the mobile NPU (Tan et al., 2024). In a diagnostic comparison, 16-bit floating-point activations lengthened the SLM Drafter’s 32-row pass from 15.7 to 38–41 ms at unchanged acceptance . The SLM’s QAT checkpoint has 2-, 4-, or 8-bit weights but computes in floating point (Gemma Team, 2026; Google DeepMind, 2026). We convert it through graph surgery and activation calibration without retraining its weights. The verifier’s MTP head is released in bfloat16 (BF16); we apply 4-bit QAT to its linear weights. Both drafters use 16-bit fixed-point activations and static graphs compiled with the Qualcomm AI Runtime (Qualcomm Technologies, Inc., 2026, QAIRT;).

For the reported collaborative configurations, activation calibration and head QAT use 60 prompts from UC-tr, the train_sft split of UltraChat 200k, not SB prompts. The head is trained for 100 steps by minimizing Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence from the BF16 head on the verifier’s greedy answers. On UC-val, this raises top-1 agreement with BF16 from 87.4% to 91.0%; 8-bit weights retain 98.8% without training but double weight storage (Appendix A).

3.3 Restricted output vocabulary

The output layers of both drafters span 262,144 tokens, and these layers and their top-kk search, repeated for every row of the SLM pass and every MTP Drafter step, take a large share of each round on the mobile device. The full vocabulary lengthens the mobile device’s time per round from 52.9 to 77.9 ms . As in FR-Spec (Zhao et al., 2025), both drafters therefore predict from one keep set of 86,089 tokens, mostly the tokens most frequent in the answers of UC-tr, plus the special and byte tokens . The MTP Drafter embeds its own drafted tokens from an 8-bit, 242 MB table of the verifier’s input embeddings for the kept tokens . Neither drafter can propose the tokens outside the keep set, which make up 3.0% of the verifier’s bonus tokens on UC-val, although UC-val is drawn from the keep set’s own dataset, and more on SB . The verifier still samples them from its full vocabulary as bonus tokens, which both drafters take as input, so the restriction costs only acceptance and exact verification stays lossless.

By the default criterion, we use the 86K keep set, whose gg of 6.23 ms is the lowest of the four sizes, against 6.44–7.57 ms, as Table 6 in Appendix D shows . The full vocabulary has the highest gg of all, as its MAT is the lowest, 2.85.

3.4 1K-token context window

Both drafters read only the last 1,024 tokens of the context, as prior drafters do on long inputs (Sadhukhan et al., 2025; Valliappan, 2026). The SLM Drafter keeps its KV cache as a ring of the last 1,024 committed tokens, or 512 in its sliding-window layers, so the mobile device never prefills more than 1,024 prompt tokens . The MTP Drafter reads the verifier’s keys and values over the same window and prefills nothing on the device, while the verifier prefills the whole prompt.

The device’s memory and prefill time set both drafters’ windows at 1,024 tokens, as UC-val’s short prompts cannot tell window lengths apart. An SLM Drafter context of 4,096 tokens instead of 1,024 moves gg from 6.82 to 6.77 ms, and MTP head windows of 512–2,048 tokens, run with the head on the server, give 7.75–7.89 ms, both within noise .

3.5 ϵ\epsilon-threshold acceptance

The quantized, restricted and windowed drafters on the mobile device propose some of the verifier’s likely tokens less often than full drafters would, and tokens outside the keep set not at all . Exact verification thus ends rounds that a plausible drafted child could have continued.

Under ϵ\epsilon-threshold acceptance , a drafted child cc of node vv is accepted if it matches the verifier’s sample or if p~​(c∣v)≥ϵ\tilde{p}(c\mid v)\geq\epsilon. Here p~\tilde{p} is the verifier’s sampling distribution after temperature scaling and top-kk/top-pp truncation, rather than its raw softmax. With a one-hot greedy distribution, the threshold adds no token beyond exact verification. The fixed threshold follows ϵ\epsilon-sampling (Hewitt et al., 2022). The verifier selects the deepest path of accepted children and appends its sample at that path’s endpoint as the bonus token . Among equally deep paths, it prefers the one with more verifier-sampled edges, then the highest product of p~\tilde{p}. This is a path-level preference, not a requirement to retain every sampled edge.

Every accepted token is in the support of p~\tilde{p}, but the rule can commit tokens that the verifier did not sample and changes their selection probabilities. It is therefore lossy: membership in the verifier’s sampling support does not guarantee distribution preservation or equivalent quality. We measure the quality–efficiency trade-off in §4.5; ϵ=1\epsilon{=}1 gives the exact-verification ablation.

Figure 3 depicts MAT against the judge score for each acceptance rule on HyCo’s tree . At ϵ=0.005\epsilon{=}0.005, applying the threshold at every node rather than only at rejections lowers gg from 5.62 to 5.10 ms at the same judge score of 60.0, and Medusa’s typical acceptance at its defaults falls below the lossless range . We choose ϵ=0.005\epsilon{=}0.005 at every node by the default criterion: it has the highest MAT and lowest gg among the screened settings, whereas ϵ=0.02\epsilon{=}0.02 matches that gg but scored 57.1 without node logging. On the fixed logged trees of one run, lowering ϵ\epsilon has little remaining headroom: ϵ=0.005\epsilon{=}0.005 gives MAT 4.364 versus 4.366 if every drafted token in the verifier’s sampling support were accepted .

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

The verifier is Gemma 4 26B-A4B (Gemma Team, 2026) with 4-bit activation-aware weight quantization (Lin et al., 2024, AWQ;), served on one RTX PRO 6000 cloud GPU. A Galaxy S26 Ultra with an SM8850 chipset runs the drafters on its Hexagon Tensor Processor v81 over a commercial LTE/5G connection; the operator assigned LTE-CA or 5G NSA during measurement. The verifier samples with temperature 1, top-kk 64 and top-pp 0.95. Thus, exact verification preserves this sampling distribution, not a fixed greedy output. All configurations use SpecEdge’s verification server (Park et al., 2025), extended with our verifier and its MTP head, the same kernels, and one client at a time (Appendix B).

4.2 Baselines and variants

Cloud+MTP uses the released BF16 MTP head over the full prefix and vocabulary, with exact verification and the same chain depth K=4K{=}4 as HyCo. SpecEdge-style drafts a 32-node tree in four sequential SLM passes, with the same 1K mobile prefill bound. SpecEdge-style + PD additionally uses proactive drafting while the verification reply is in flight; both variants verify exactly. SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon keeps this SLM-only construction but applies exactly the same threshold and path-selection rule as HyCo. This controls the acceptance rule, not output quality; we therefore compare their quality directly.

HyCo uses one SLM pass; HyCo-2P uses two. Both apply ϵ=0.005\epsilon{=}0.005. HyCo exact sets ϵ=1\epsilon{=}1, which adds no token that the verifier would not sample. The server-head variant also verifies exactly but leaves the head on the server, in BF16 with the 86K keep set and 1K window, and omits runner-up siblings. It is an alternative configuration, not a placement-only ablation (Table 5). On-device 8K is the SLM alone with an 8K context, full vocabulary, and greedy decoding, evaluated on SB only; it represents standalone local generation, not a matched drafter ablation.

4.3 Evaluation and uncertainty

We use all 480 Spec-Bench questions (Xia et al., 2024, SB-480;) to measure decoding efficiency, including both MT-bench turns, with a 1,024-token output cap. To assess the effect of ϵ\epsilon-threshold acceptance on the generated answers, we add the following quality evaluations. GPT-5.4 scores first-turn answers from 0 to 100 using the question, not a reference answer. The aggregate judge score covers non-QA tasks; QA diagnostics are reported separately in Appendix E. Two summarization items consistently refused by the judge’s filter are also omitted. Thus, HyCo–Cloud+MTP quality comparisons cover 398 questions. Complete-case three-run comparisons involving SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon cover 396, owing to two additional missing scores across its runs (Appendix E). Reference metrics supplement this question-only judge.

For ∞\inftyBench Sum, we evaluate the first 50 English novels in HELMET’s seed-42 order, truncated to 32K tokens with its preprocessing (Zhang et al., 2024; Yen et al., 2025), with a 1,200-token output cap. We report ROUGE-L-Sum (Lin, 2004) and HELMET’s model-based fluency-weighted F1, key-point recall, and precision using GPT-5.4. Precision tests support in the expert summary, not direct factual verification against the entire novel.

We measure GPU time per output token gg, including prompt prefill; MAT; and delivery speed, pooled output tokens divided by mobile wall time from request start to last token. Mobile draft time excludes verification waits and prefill. HyCo and SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon each have three SB generations, with one judge evaluation per output; other configurations, the 32K set, and Cloud+MTP have one. Reported ±\pm values are the sample SD of run-level measurements, not confidence intervals.

Paired 95% CIs use 2,000 question-level bootstrap samples, clustering MT-bench turns. For repeated quality, we first average each question’s three scores and then resample common questions. These intervals condition on the recorded generations and the single Cloud+MTP run; they do not separate generation variation from judge variation (Appendix E).

4.4 Efficiency under matched acceptance rules

Under the same ϵ\epsilon rule, HyCo reduces GPU time by 38.6±0.238.6\pm 0.2% on SB versus 29.6±0.229.6\pm 0.2% for SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon, an additional 9.0 percentage points. Delivery speeds are 35.0±0.735.0\pm 0.7 and 18.9±0.118.9\pm 0.1 tokens/s, respectively. The hybrid tree achieves MAT 4.71 with one SLM pass, whereas the SLM-only tree reaches 4.13 with four. On 32K summarization, their reductions are 29.2% (95% CI: 27.8–30.6%) and 15.7% (14.1–17.1%), at 21.0 and 12.4 tokens/s.

The benefit also appears without relaxation. On SB, HyCo exact reduces gg by 27.7%, compared with 20.6% for SpecEdge-style exact. On 32K, the corresponding savings are 11.9% and 2.9%. The exact and same-ϵ\epsilon comparisons therefore provide complementary evidence: the design saves server work without altering the sampling distribution, and an additional advantage remains when both device drafters share the relaxed rule.

HyCo-2P saves more server time, 44.7%/31.9% on SB/32K, but delivers fewer tokens per second than default HyCo. The server-head configuration is faster on SB, at 36.1 tokens/s, but saves only 14.6% of server GPU time. PD raises SpecEdge-style’s SB saving from 20.6% to 23.9%, but lowers delivery from 16.1 to 12.1 tokens/s. On 32K, both save 2.9% (rounded), while PD lowers delivery from 10.0 to 8.2 tokens/s. Thus, neither more passes nor overlapping draft work is uniformly beneficial in this deployment.

Per-question analysis finds 2, 1, and 0 non-saving cases among the 480 questions in HyCo’s three runs. They are short RAG answers of about 40 tokens. Pooled gg weights questions by each configuration’s output length and is not the mean per-question reduction (Appendix F).

4.5 Quality and failure cases

The three run-level judge means are 90.34±0.5090.34\pm 0.50 for HyCo and 90.60±0.6190.60\pm 0.61 for SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon. Their paired difference on common questions is −0.2-0.2 points (95% CI: −1.2-1.2 to +0.8+0.8). Relative to Cloud+MTP, HyCo differs by +0.2+0.2 points (−0.9-0.9 to +1.3+1.3). Against HyCo exact, its three-run per-question mean differs by −0.4-0.4 points (−1.5-1.5 to +0.6+0.6), using the same 398 questions and one exact run. Intervals spanning zero do not establish quality equivalence.

Translation is an important exception to the aggregate pattern: HyCo scores 2.6 points below SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon (95% CI: −5.2-5.2 to −0.2-0.2), while its difference from Cloud+MTP spans zero. SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon is higher in all three translation runs. The 15 task-wise contrasts are exploratory and unadjusted for multiple comparisons; we do not claim that every task is unaffected (Table 8).

Reference-based checks also cover HyCo’s first SB generation. For HyCo versus Cloud+MTP, GSM8K numeric-answer accuracy is 95.0% versus 95.0%, RAG contains-gold accuracy is 65.7% versus 67.1%, CNN/DailyMail ROUGE-L is 19.2 versus 19.8, and WMT14 corpus BLEU is 33.9 versus 33.7. These are descriptive single-generation comparisons, not three-run averages; RAG measures normalized reference containment, not full answer correctness (Appendix E).

On 32K summaries, HyCo’s HELMET F1 difference from Cloud+MTP is +0.4+0.4 points (−2.3-2.3 to +3.1+3.1), and its precision difference is +1.9+1.9 (−2.6-2.6 to +6.2+6.2). ROUGE-L-Sum is 37.5 versus 38.5, a difference of −1.0-1.0 (−2.1-2.1 to +0.1+0.1). SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon instead combines higher precision with lower recall (Table 9). These reference-based measures add evidence about summary content but are not a guarantee of factual consistency.

A fixed ±20\pm 20-point screen of HyCo’s three-run per-question means against Cloud+MTP selects 13 decreases and 12 increases. Our manual inspection identifies six substantive errors among the decreases, as well as score/content discrepancies in both directions. We retain all measured scores; the selected cases are not an estimate of the overall error rate (Appendix F).

4.6 Mobile costs and head transfer

On SB, HyCo delivers 35.0 tokens/s versus 26.4 for the SLM alone. Its 12.1 ms of mobile draft time per output token is about a third of the SLM alone’s 36.8 ms. SpecEdge-style exact delivers 16.1 tokens/s and consumes 42.8 ms of mobile draft time per token. The two efficiency goals therefore use distinct references: less server work than Cloud+MTP, and faster delivery than the local SLM. Since Cloud+MTP was not streamed to the phone, we do not compare its user delivery speed with HyCo.

In a separate paired 150-question experiment, the device-head configuration (W4, 86K keep set, 1K window) has 4.0% lower MAT than the original BF16 server head (95% CI: 3.0–4.9%). In the full SB experiment, relaxing HyCo exact raises MAT from 3.84 to 4.71. These are separate comparisons, not additive estimates of independent component effects.

The first hand-off introduces a startup cost. Single-run HyCo traces have mean time to first token of 846 ms on SB and 4.60 s on 32K inputs. Thus, higher average delivery speed does not imply a lower first-token delay. We report GPU-busy efficiency, not loaded-service capacity or energy savings (Appendix G).

5 Discussion

5.1 From server accelerator to client drafter

Device–cloud systems commonly offload an independent draft model (Park et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026c). When the server already has a native draft head, the remaining server-side opportunity can be small (Lyu et al., 2026). HyCo changes the work split itself: it moves the native head’s sequential steps to the mobile device and returns the slice of verifier state that the head reads. MTP self-speculation becomes a device–cloud protocol rather than only a server-internal accelerator.

This split is useful when server GPU time is a priority and the head’s inputs fit the link. The UC-val comparison in §3.1 exchanges about 5 ms of server time per round for about 20 ms of additional mobile work, while the independent SLM supplies alternative branches without taking over the chain’s depth . Our single-client measurements establish the execution-time trade-off, not the capacity gain of a loaded service.

5.2 Choosing the mobile–cloud work split

The configurations expose different operating points. Prior systems adapt draft length to the channel (Li et al., 2026c), an acceptance threshold (Li et al., 2026b), or which tokens reach the server (Wang et al., 2025). Here, the choices also include where the native head executes and how many SLM passes accompany it. Figure 1 illustrates the associated deployment priorities, rather than an evaluated online switching policy.

More drafting is not uniformly beneficial. The second SLM pass in HyCo-2P exchanges more mobile work for a larger server saving, at 29.0 tokens/s on SB-480 against 35.0 for default HyCo . On ∞\inftyBench Sum, however, that pass adds only 2.7 percentage points of server saving and reduces delivery speed by 10%: its MAT gain is smaller, and prefill, which drafting does not shorten, accounts for about a fifth of gg .

Cloud+MTP removes mobile drafting altogether. Among the exact configurations, server head uses 9.2 ms of mobile draft time per output token versus 14.7 ms for HyCo exact, with 13.1 percentage points less server saving on SB . The preferred split depends on which resource is constrained; time measurements alone do not determine an energy-optimal choice.

5.3 Lossy acceptance revisited

Wang et al. (2026) identify risks of truncation-based verification: an allowed set constrains which tokens can be accepted, but does not preserve the verifier’s relative preferences within that set. Our ϵ\epsilon-threshold acceptance belongs to this category. The repeated and long-summary results in §4.5 characterize its trade-off on the evaluated tasks; they do not remove the underlying distributional risk.

The exact comparisons favor HyCo over the SLM-only baseline on both SB and 32K inputs, while the same-ϵ\epsilon comparisons retain an efficiency advantage after matching the relaxed rule. The latter controls the acceptance rule but not the proposal distribution. Its overall score interval and translation difference support a task-dependent trade-off.

The fixed-tree UC-val replay of §3.5 helps explain which proposals benefit. About two thirds of threshold-only accepted tokens come from the verifier’s MTP chain, a tenth from runner-up siblings, and a quarter from the SLM . Thus, most such tokens follow the native head’s proposals rather than an independent drafter’s. This composition, the use of p~\tilde{p} rather than raw softmax, and the path-level preference for sampled edges are plausible explanations for the observed scores, not guarantees of quality. The replay follows fixed logged trajectories and does not measure the quality of newly generated answers.

6 Conclusion

HyCo combines two complementary drafters on a mobile NPU: the verifier’s native MTP head supplies depth, and one SLM pass supplies alternative branches. Returning the head’s inputs instead of executing its sequential steps reduces server work, while the hybrid tree avoids repeated SLM passes for depth. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a bounded context make this split practical on the device.

In single-client measurements, HyCo with ϵ\epsilon-threshold acceptance reduces server GPU time per output token against Cloud+MTP by 38.6% on SB and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization; with exact verification, it still saves 27.7% and 11.9%, respectively. On SB, it delivers tokens 32.5% faster than the SLM alone at a third of its mobile draft time per output token. Exact-verification and same-ϵ\epsilon comparisons support the design, while repeated generation and summary assessment quantify a task-dependent quality–efficiency trade-off. Hybrid drafting therefore offers a practical mobile–cloud operating point without requiring the SLM alone to provide both depth and alternatives. Applying the same split to other model families is a natural next step; it requires a native head that the mobile device can run, and Appendix H shows the SLM Drafter working for Muse-Glimmer-30B through a token bridge without retraining.

Limitations

Deployment scope and cost.

Each round waits for one network round trip, which bounds mobile delivery speed. Retaining unverified device tokens, as in Synera (Wang et al., 2025), would introduce a different lossy mechanism. The full hybrid deployment uses one mobile device, one commercial cellular network, one cloud GPU type, and one verifier family. All configurations serve one client at a time in our engine. We measure GPU execution time and mobile draft time, not loaded-service capacity, monetary cost, or device and radio energy.

Distribution and quality.

Default HyCo does not preserve the verifier’s sampling distribution. The reported judge-score interval permits a modest quality decrease. The aggregate covers scored non-QA first-turn answers, not QA or second-turn quality. Translation favors SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon in an exploratory comparison. The question-only judge and reference-summary-based HELMET metrics do not comprehensively assess factual consistency, and we do not establish how relaxed acceptance changes output diversity. Only the two main relaxed systems have three SB generations; the other configurations and Cloud+MTP have one. Question-bootstrap intervals condition on these outputs, and one judge evaluation per output does not separate judging from generation variability. The UC-val screening range is not an equivalence margin. Appendices A and D distinguish calibration and development data from the reported benchmark runs.

Requirements and device costs.

HyCo requires access to the verifier’s native head, intermediate hidden states, and KV entries, which may not be available from closed model services; its head must also run on the mobile device, and the SLM needs a shared tokenizer or token bridge. Heads that read more verifier layers (Chen et al., 2026) can require a larger hand-off. The MTP Drafter adds about 20 ms per mobile round and up to 6.3 MB to the first reply of a long prompt. The device stores 365 MB for it alongside the SLM’s 754 MB graph .

Vocabulary, context, and input scope.

The UC-derived keep set and 1K window need not suit every language or domain (Abramovich et al., 2026). Tokens outside the keep set comprise 3.0% of verifier bonus tokens on UC-val and 6.8% on the 150-question SB subset of the head-configuration comparison (§4.6) . Exact verification preserves the output distribution despite these proposal restrictions; relaxed acceptance does not. The SLM accesses earlier context only indirectly through the MTP chain. We evaluate text only, not Gemma’s image or audio inputs.

Information exposure.

Each client holds the MTP head and part of the verifier’s input embeddings. Transmitted activations and reply-size patterns may expose information beyond the text (Cunningham, 2026). We evaluate no safeguard.

Appendix A The Drafters on the Mobile Device

Table 3 shows each drafter’s integer formats, size and training. Weights are per-channel symmetric integers at the bit maps it lists, activation ranges are fixed ahead of time, and no operator falls back to floating point. QAIRT compiles static shapes, with 32 tree rows for the SLM Drafter and one query position over a 1,024-column window for the MTP Drafter.

Final calibration and training.

The collaborative configurations in Table 2 use the UC-tr-calibrated SLM and, where applicable, MTP head. Both calibration procedures use 60 first-turn prompts from the training split of UltraChat 200k and the verifier’s greedy answers; no SB prompt is used in this calibration or QAT. The keep-set token counts use separate UC-tr conversations. Validation and benchmark configurations are distinguished below.

The graph surgery of the SLM Drafter keeps the checkpoint’s bit allocation and the weights’ integers and scales bit-exact, rewrites each low-bit weight matrix multiplication as an integer one with an explicit encoding of its bit width, decomposes root-mean-square (RMS) normalization into standard operators, computes the rotary tables on the host, and keeps the embedding tables on the CPU as lookup tables . For the final calibration, activation ranges come from the 60 UC-tr prompts with the verifier’s greedy answers used for the MTP head’s QAT, and KV caches use 8 bits with a range of 1.2 times their 99.9th percentile . Keys enter the KV ring with their rotary embedding applied, so an entry keeps its absolute position wherever it sits in the ring .

Table 4 shows the UC-tr training settings for the MTP head, whose KL loss follows Gemma’s own QAT (Gemma Team, 2025) and data-free QAT for LLMs (Liu et al., 2024b). After a per-channel search for the clipping ratio that minimizes the quantization error, every linear layer is fake-quantized with a straight-through estimator (Bengio et al., 2013). The training inputs, captured by teacher forcing the verifier in BF16, are the input embedding, the last hidden state, and the keys and values of the two source layers . The 60 UC-tr prompts are first turns sampled at random from conversations that the keep set’s counts never read. The top-1 agreement of §3.2 compares the quantized integer head with the BF16 head on the 25,625 response tokens of the 60 UC-val sequences. The trained integers and scales form a static graph whose output layer is untied and restricted to the keep set, and whose fixed input ranges are the 99.99th percentiles of the UC-tr captures.

The keep set always holds the 24 special tokens, the 256 byte tokens, which can spell any string, and all 4,678 Hangul tokens regardless of their UC-tr frequency . The other 81,131 are the tokens most frequent in the assistant turns of 20,000 UC-tr conversations. The SLM Drafter’s input tables stay complete, and the MTP Drafter’s first step reads e⁡(xt+1)e(x_{t+1}) from the hand-off, so both drafters can take a committed token outside the keep set.

The hand-off carries the MTP Drafter’s inputs as 8-bit integers . These are e⁡(xt+1)e(x_{t+1}) and hth_{t}, the latter taken before the verifier’s final normalization, 5,632 values per round, and the keys and values of the last full-attention and the last sliding-window layer, 6,144 values per committed token. The first reply seeds the MTP Drafter’s window with the prompt’s last 1,024 tokens, at most 6.3 MB .

Appendix B Verifier Engine

We ported the verifier’s text model with static shapes into SpecEdge’s server (Park et al., 2025), replacing its model side, and checked it against the Hugging Face model . Attention projections run as 4-bit integer Marlin matrix products (Frantar et al., 2025) and the experts, 8 of 128 per token, through vLLM’s fused Marlin mixture-of-experts kernel (Kwon et al., 2023), while the dense MLP and the router stay in 16 bits. RMS normalization runs in FlashInfer (Ye et al., 2025), and attention in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) with the tree mask. Tree verification uses the routed MoE kernel described above rather than a dense all-expert path. Each decode round is padded to the narrowest of ten attention windows that covers its context, 256, 512 and 768 positions and then powers of two up to the maximum context of 65,536, and replays that window’s CUDA graphs, while prefill runs eagerly in chunks . The verifier’s MTP head, which Cloud+MTP and the server head variant run on the server, replays its own graphs over the same windows, and its chains agree with eager execution on 99.2–99.6% of tokens, as often as two stock attention kernels agree.

Appendix C Decoding Round and Configurations

Algorithms 1–4 specify one HyCo decoding round as implemented. Algorithm 1 is the round, and it calls the MTP Drafter (Algorithm 2), the construction of the hybrid draft tree (Algorithm 3) and the verification (Algorithm 4). Every HyCo configuration uses chain depth K=4K{=}4, runner-up siblings at depths up to D=2D{=}2, node budget B=32B{=}32, depth cost ln⁡λ\ln\lambda with λ=0.66\lambda{=}0.66, W=1,024W{=}1{,}024-token windows, the keep set 𝒱\mathcal{V} of 86,089 tokens and 32 SLM Drafter candidates per row, and ϵ=0.005\epsilon{=}0.005 except in the exact variant. Positions count from 0, so the root xt+1x_{t+1} sits at position tt, and p~\tilde{p} applies temperature 1, top-kk 64 and top-pp 0.95.

At a request’s start, the mobile device fills the SLM Drafter’s cache with the prompt’s last WW tokens and drafts the first tree with the SLM Drafter alone, while the server prefills the whole prompt; its first HH thus carries up to WW rows, and later ones carry only the newly committed positions. Since p~​(c∣v)≥1\tilde{p}(c\mid v)\geq 1 only when p~(⋅∣v)\tilde{p}(\cdot\mid v) puts all its mass on cc, ϵ=1\epsilon{=}1 reduces line 6 of Algorithm 4 to exact verification.

Table 5 shows the settings of every configuration in Tables 2 and 7.

Appendix D Validation Protocol and Measurement Conditions

The configuration comparisons of §3 use UC-val on the cloud GPU and include prefill in gg, as the benchmark runs do . UC-val has 60 prompts, about 100 tokens at the median, and a 512-token output limit. Earlier SB trials informed implementation development and were rechecked on UC-val . The final 86K keep set is derived from UC-tr, and ϵ\epsilon was chosen on UC-val before the final benchmark runs. The development-stage sweeps below compare their listed configurations within each block; they are not repetitions of the final benchmark configuration.

These runs, including those of Table 6 for the keep set and the two window lengths, took place in different sessions and setups . The runs on the siblings, the keep set and the SLM Drafter’s context used the development-stage 45K keep set, which the keep-set block varies, and exact verification . The head-window block kept the head on the server, restricted to a 55K superset of the 45K set . The runs on the rule, Medusa’s setting, the threshold and the passes ran with the 86K keep set and runner-up siblings at depths 1–2 in one session . In that session, ϵ=0.02\epsilon{=}0.02 at every node scored 57.1 without node logging and 61.5 with every tree node logged .

The lossless range of §3 runs from 58.7, the score of Cloud+MTP in an earlier session without the mobile device, to 63.0, one of the scores of ϵ=1\epsilon{=}1, exact, on HyCo’s tree in three sessions, 61.8, 63.0 and 60.2 .

The quantization follows the NPU and the released checkpoints, so no UC-val run chose it. The score penalty of §3.1 is measured rather than chosen. It is ln⁡0.66≈−0.42\ln 0.66\approx-0.42, where 0.66 is the geometric mean of the chain’s per-depth acceptance rates in §3.1, measured over 7,513 rounds with exact verification and the MTP Drafter on the mobile device .

In the test runs, gg includes the prompt’s prefill, which configurations with a mobile tree run as a separate step before their first round, and counts Cloud+MTP’s tokens up to its first stop token, as the mobile device does .

On ∞\inftyBench Sum, the 32K setting uses the first 50 novels of HELMET’s seed-42 order with its 2-shot prompt, and its prompts have a median of 30.6K Gemma tokens . Answers are sampled, not greedily decoded as in HELMET. During the test runs, the mobile device keeps its screen on at minimum brightness. Temperature was not controlled or used to adjust the reported full-run timings. With the screen off, each round trip took 14 ms longer .

Appendix E Quality per Task

Scoring and missing observations.

The SB judge sees the question and answer, each truncated to 6,000 characters by our scoring script, but not a reference answer. We retain the original scores and do not replace scores after manual inspection. Two summarization prompts are consistently blocked by the judge’s filter. HyCo has 398 eligible scored first turns in each run; SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon has 397, 397, and 398. The latter’s three-run complete-case intersection has 396 questions. Consequently, HyCo–Cloud+MTP uses 398 paired questions, while both repeated comparisons involving SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon use 396. The final PD run provides 558 of 560 SB turns (479 questions), with 398 eligible first-turn judge scores, and 49 of 50 long-summary requests and scores. A failed score or incomplete response is not imputed.

Bootstrap procedure.

The release uses 2,000 percentile-bootstrap draws with seed 20261011 restarted per contrast, with question IDs sorted as strings. Both MT-bench turns are resampled together for efficiency. Repeated quality averages all three available scores per question before complete-case pairing and resampling. These intervals reflect variation across recorded questions conditional on the observed runs; they are not an estimate of variability across arbitrary deployments. The separate run SD combines generation and judging variability because each output has only one judge evaluation. Intervals may differ slightly from intermediate logs whose random-number streams were consumed in another order.

QA diagnostics.

The question-only judge is not a reference-based QA accuracy test, so we report QA separately from the non-QA aggregate. Our NQ-Open reference matching procedure matched 43 of the 80 QA questions; the remaining 37 were unmatched. Using the same normalized reference-containment rule as for RAG, Cloud+MTP scores 30.2%, HyCo 30.2%, HyCo exact 25.6%, and SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon 29.5% on these 43 items. For the two repeated systems, each question’s three binary scores are averaged; the other systems use one answer. The HyCo–Cloud+MTP difference is 0.0 percentage points (95% CI: −13.2-13.2 to +10.9+10.9). Unmatched questions are omitted from this diagnostic rather than counted as errors; containment is not strict exact match. The question-only QA judge means, covering all 80 questions, are 49.1 for HyCo and 45.1 for Cloud+MTP; they do not establish reference-answer correctness.

Reference metrics.

The optional reference-metric script computes WMT14 corpus BLEU, CNN/DailyMail ROUGE-L, GSM8K numeric-answer accuracy, RAG contains-gold accuracy, and InfiniteBench ROUGE-L-Sum. The RAG measure checks normalized reference containment, not full answer correctness. For a descriptive check on HyCo’s first generation, GSM8K accuracy is 95.0% for both HyCo and Cloud+MTP; RAG accuracy is 65.7% versus 67.1%; ROUGE-L is 19.2 versus 19.8; BLEU is 33.9 versus 33.7. These values refer to one output set, not the three-run judge aggregate. On 32K summaries, the recorded ROUGE-L-Sum differences are −1.0-1.0 [−2.1-2.1, +0.1+0.1] for HyCo and −0.8-0.8 [−1.8-1.8, +0.1+0.1] for SpecEdge-ϵ\epsilon. For SpecEdge-style and PD, the differences are −0.2-0.2 [−1.0-1.0, +0.4+0.4] and −0.8-0.8 [−2.0-2.0, +0.2+0.2], on 50 and 49 paired summaries, respectively.

The HELMET evaluation retains its book-summary prompts and key points, using GPT-5.4 as the judge. One metric evaluation contains separate fluency, recall, and precision requests, not three independent repeated evaluations of the same metric. The script requests temperature 0.1, top-pp 0.9 and seed 42, omitting a field only if the API rejects it. The reported comparisons use the recorded scores, not new API calls.

Appendix F Failure Cases

Server cost.

Among 480 questions, HyCo has 2, 1, and 0 cases with Δ​g≥0\Delta g\geq 0 in its three runs. The non-saving cases are short RAG answers of approximately 40 tokens. This observation illustrates an unfavorable operating condition; it does not establish that output length alone causes every cost difference.

Quality-screened cases.

We apply a fixed ±20\pm 20-point screen to the difference between each question’s three-run HyCo mean and Cloud+MTP’s single score. This selects 13 decreases and 12 increases. The following categories are our own judgments, not an independent adjudication or the overall error rate.

Seven selected decreases have one especially low-scoring HyCo generation. In one inspected question (559), identical answer text received scores of 15 and 95, showing that at least some large changes can originate in the evaluator rather than different text. This does not establish that all score discrepancies are judge errors.

Appendix G System Metrics and Reproducibility

Table 11 separates GPU execution efficiency from user-visible delivery. Per request, gg includes server_ms plus prefill_ms. Cloud+MTP already includes prefill in the former, so the latter is zero. Mobile draft time is phone_ms minus verify_wait_ms and phone_prefill_ms, divided by output tokens. All ratios pool numerators and denominators before averaging across repeated runs. For PD, subtracting the verification wait also excludes any drafting overlapped with that wait, so the mobile-time column is not its total active compute.

PD recording coverage.

The SB PD run contains 558 of 560 scheduled turns; its paired efficiency contrast uses 479 common questions. Two recorded turns (questions 559 and 560) have no assigned PRIME prefill and retain prefill_ms=0. We do not impute these times, so reported PD GPU time may be slightly underestimated. On 32K, PD completes 49 of 50 requests; its efficiency and quality contrasts use those 49 common questions. Other finalized long-summary configurations have 50 records.

First-token latency.

The recorded single-run latency export reports HyCo mean/p90 TTFT of 846/1,922 ms on SB and 4,604/4,842 ms on 32K summaries. For HyCo-2P these are 967/2,147 ms and 3,759/3,908 ms, and for HyCo exact 920/2,050 ms and 4,014/4,344 ms. Recorded SB summaries put network and serialization at roughly 40–58 ms per round, after subtracting server decoding from the verification wait; this is not a standalone link-RTT measurement. These are individual-run traces, not three-run averages; other finalized configurations do not have a corresponding released per-event latency trace. The initial head-state transfer can contain up to 1,024 positions. Consequently, first-token latency must be considered separately from average delivery speed.

Appendix H Additional Cross-Family Measurements

The SLM half of the Hybrid Drafter is not tied to Gemma 4. In additional runs, our SLM Drafter drafted without retraining on a Galaxy Z Fold8 smartphone, which shares the S26 Ultra’s SM8850 chipset, for Muse-Glimmer-30B in NVFP4 (Meta Superintelligence Lab, 2026; NVIDIA, 2026), a verifier of another family whose tokenizer it is mapped to through a token bridge. Glimmer’s own DFlash2 head (Chen et al., 2026; Inco AI, 2026), which reads five of its layers and was not deployed on the device, drafted eight-token chains on the server, as in our server head variant . Over all 480 SB questions, a SpecEdge-style tree of four SLM passes and 127 nodes (128 verifier rows, against 33 in Table 5) reached an MAT of 3.16, and a 32-node tree of the chain and a single SLM pass reached 4.07.

These runs used another verifier, server GPU, and engine, and answers of up to 2,048 tokens, so they are not comparable with Table 2, but they show that the SLM Drafter carries over to another model family through a token bridge. A head that the mobile device can run for such families would move the whole Hybrid Drafter, not only its SLM half, to the device, which we leave to future work.

Appendix I Artifacts, Licenses and Compute

Table 12 shows the models, data and software we used, with the license that each distributor declares . We use each artifact as intended: the models for inference, the benchmarks for evaluation, and UC only for the uses in Table 12. The one model we train, the MTP Drafter, is a derivative that its Apache 2.0 license permits. The SpecEdge engine permits research and evaluation but needs a separate license for commercial deployment, and the Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) passages in SB are licensed for noncommercial use only. Our use is noncommercial research. The test data are public and in English, except for the German source sentences of SB’s translation category.

For the main Gemma deployment, weight training is the MTP head’s QAT: 100 steps of about 1.5 s each on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The final-run records account for 5.04 GPU-busy hours and 31.00 cumulative mobile-request hours. These sums are not the full development budget: they exclude setup, idle time, failed requests absent from the records, calibration, validation sweeps, and additional cross-family experiments. The final GPU is a 96 GB RTX PRO 6000 in an AWS g7e.2xlarge instance.
